question_text: Identify the theme. Composer Mark Snow created this unforgettable TV theme using early 1990s synthesizer gear, but its most famous sound effect was a complete accident. The Whistle: the famous haunting whistle was a combination of an E-mu Proteus 2 synth patch ("Whistling Joe") blended with a recorded sample of Snow's wife, Glynn, whistling. The Echo Effect: show creator Chris Carter kept rejecting Snow's early theme ideas for being too conventional. Frustrated, Snow slammed his hand and forearm down onto his keyboard, triggering an echo/delay effect on a patch he had open; he immediately loved the haunting, repetitive echo, added the whistle over top, and Carter approved it instantly.

Identify X and Y. The artistic partnership between director X and actor Y is one of the most legendary in cinematic history: they made 16 films together, defining post-war cinema and reshaping global filmmaking, yet after their last movie A the duo never worked together again. During the two years of production of A, X did not allow Y to shave or cut his hair, preventing Y from taking other roles while Y's own newly launched production studio neared bankruptcy. When X was fired from a famous movie B for defending his decision to cast non-professional actors, Y publicly declared X's disrespect for professional actors a challenge to all national professional actors and said he would never work with X again. To pay off studio debts, Y took high-paying roles including Westerns, TV shows, and lower-tier action flicks, which X viewed as a betrayal of his talent. In February 1993 the two old men met for the last time at a mutual friend's funeral; X asked, "Are you okay? Don't overdo it, now," and Y quietly replied, "I'm okay." X used to say he wanted to praise Y if he ever saw him again but never got the chance. Y passed away on Christmas Eve 1997; X died nine months later in September 1998.
answer_text: X - Akira Kurosawa; Y - Toshiro Mifune

question_text: Identify X and Y. The opening of the original series "The Bridge" features one of the most famous premises in television history. On a pitch-black night, the streetlights on the massive bridge connecting X and Y suddenly shut off; when they turn back on, a maintenance crew discovers a woman's body laid flat across the border line between X and Y. Police from both X and Y arrive simultaneously and argue over jurisdiction, until officers attempt to lift the corpse and discover the killer did not leave a single body - they severed two different women at the torso and stitched them together: the top half a high-profile politician from X, the bottom half a sex worker from Y who had gone missing a year prior. This forces the two police departments into an uneasy joint operation, kicking off the iconic cat-and-mouse hunt for a killer known as the "Truth Terrorist."

Identify X and Y. While it's a popular urban legend that network A cancelled show X to fund show Y, that isn't quite what happened, though X played a direct role in how Y came to exist. Season 1 of X cost an unprecedented $100 million for 12 episodes (about $8.3 million an episode), filmed on a 5-acre backlot at Cinecitta Studios in Italy, making it the most expensive TV series in history at the time. X was a joint co-production between network A and a foreign broadcaster B; after Season 1, B could not afford to keep funding it and A was left to bear the cost alone, so A cancelled X. While X didn't die to fund Y, it proved to A's executives that audiences would tune in for adult-oriented, grand-scale worldbuilding with political intrigue, complex morality, violence and explicit drama, taught A a budget lesson for Y's Season 1, and established a talent/production pipeline that fed directly into Y.
answer_text: X - Rome; Y - Game of Thrones

In X, the director made a deliberate choice in casting and credits: rather than listing character names corresponding to the real-life Muhammad Abdul Aziz and Khalil Islam, he explicitly credited them under different names - Thomas Hayer (played by Giancarlo Esposito, also known as Thomas Hagan/Talmadge Hayer/Mujahid Abdul Halim), Ben Thomas (Wendell Pierce), William Bradley (Michael Guess, later known as Al-Mustafa Shabazz), Wilbur Kinley (Leland Gantt), and Leon Davis (Leonard Thomas).
answer_text: Malcolm X. The real Newark Nation of Islam hitmen were named in sworn affidavits as the actual assassins by Thomas Hagan, who testified that Muhammad Abdul Aziz (Norman Butler) and Khalil Islam (Thomas Johnson) were completely innocent; the court ignored this and convicted all three, and the case was not reopened when Hagan resubmitted affidavits in 1977/78. In November 2021, a formal re-investigation by the Manhattan DA confirmed the NYPD and FBI had withheld exculpatory evidence, and Muhammad Abdul Aziz and the late Khalil Islam were officially exonerated.

question_text: Identify X/A and Y. The story behind a famous chant X (commonly known as A) is one of the most famous cases of music exploitation. The original song, 'Mbube', was written and recorded in 1939 in Johannesburg by Zulu singer Solomon Linda and his group The Evening Birds; its vocal hook, a Zulu phrase, was misheard by westerners as X. Linda sold the master recording rights to Gallo Record Company for a paltry 10 shillings and didn't realize he was signing away his rights. In the 1950s, Pete Seeger and The Weavers transcribed the chant as X and made it a hit; in 1961 the doo-wop group The Tokens added English lyrics, turning it into A, a global #1 hit. Solomon Linda died in 1962 with $25 in his bank account, leaving his daughters in poverty. Three decades later, studio B used X in the movie Y, which became a soundtrack and box-office megahit generating an estimated $15 million in royalties for B. In 2000, journalist Rian Malan exposed how Linda's family had been robbed of millions, leading to a 2004 lawsuit against B using a 1911 Commonwealth copyright law under which rights revert to a composer's heirs 25 years after death. In February 2006, B and Abilene Music agreed to a global settlement awarding a lump sum and future royalties for A, and Solomon Linda was legally recognized worldwide as a co-composer of A for the first time.
answer_text: X - O Wimoweh, A - The Lion Sleeps Tonight; Y - The Lion King
